0.0.n: Sets up the initial plan before circumstances changed.

0.1.n: 家族３人 describes the family as a group of three.

0.2.n: 人 counts people; here it gives the number of family members.

0.3.n: Marks the group taking part in the outing.

0.4.n: This form of 行く expresses intention when followed by と思う.

0.5.n: Marks 行こう as the content of the speaker's thought.

0.6.n: 思う in the past ていた form describes an intention held before the change.

0.7.n: Adds an explanatory tone before the polite ending です.

0.8.n: Makes the explanation polite; the past time is already expressed in 思っていた.

0.9.n: Connects the original plan to the unexpected change that follows.

1.0.n: A conventional way to refer to one's own husband.

1.1.n: Marks the husband as the person who became ill in the next line.

1.2.n: Short for 万国博覧会, an international exposition.

1.3.n: Marks the Expo as the destination of 行く.

1.4.n: The plain form is used before a time expression with 前, even when describing past events.

1.5.n: Gives the amount of time before the planned visit.

1.6.n: 行く１週間前 places the event one week earlier than the planned visit.

1.7.n: Marks one week before the visit as the time when he became ill.

2.1.n: The medical name for inflammation of the appendix.

2.3.n: Links the disease's name to the general noun 病気.

2.4.n: 病気になる is the usual expression for becoming ill.

2.5.n: Marks 病気 as the resulting state with なる.

2.6.n: A linking form of なる that connects this event to the next clause.

3.0.n: 行ける means can go; its negative form 行けない changes to 行けなく before なる.

3.1.n: Polite past form of なる; with 行けなく, it describes losing the ability to go.

4.0.n: Points back to appendicitis and directly modifies 病気.

4.1.n: Refers to the appendicitis mentioned earlier.

4.2.n: Marks this disease as the topic of the explanation.

4.5.n: Literally the cecum, but commonly used as an everyday name for appendicitis.

4.7.n: Links 盲腸 to 名前 to identify the alternative name.

4.8.n: Refers to the everyday label 盲腸 rather than a person's name.

4.9.n: Marks the name under which the disease is known.

4.10.n: Adds this alternative name alongside the medical name already given.

4.11.n: Passive 知られる plus ています politely describes an established state of being known.

5.0.n: An everyday term for the abdominal area, not specifically the stomach organ.

5.1.n: Marks the belly as what becomes painful.

5.3.n: 痛い changes to 痛く before なる to describe a change in condition.

5.4.n: Combines with 痛く to describe the onset of pain.

5.5.n: The preceding description tells us what kind of illness it is.

5.6.n: Politely finishes the explanation identifying it as an illness.

0.lit: Originally, as a family of three, we had been thinking we would go, but…
0.tip: 行こうと思っていた expresses a previously held intention or plan.

1.lit: My husband, one week before going to the Expo…
1.tip: The husband's が connects to becoming ill in the next line; the time phrase comes between.

2.lit: Became ill with a disease called appendicitis, and…
2.tip: という introduces a name: 虫垂炎という病気 means an illness called appendicitis.

3.tip: A negative ability form followed by なる expresses becoming unable to do something.

4.lit: This disease is also known by the name 盲腸.
4.tip: Here 盲腸 is the everyday name for appendicitis, although its literal anatomical meaning is cecum.

5.lit: It is an illness in which the belly becomes very painful.
5.tip: The whole phrase お腹がとても痛くなる comes before 病気 to describe the illness.
